messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 25-year-old journalist who came to treatment after months of trying to make his life smaller and quieter. He is a young African man living in the United States, in a relationship, and until the incident he described himself as someone who loved being out in the world, noticing things, asking questions, and turning what he saw into stories. The trauma he returns to began while he was working. He had been covering a police-related event and was close enough to hear the movement around him in sharp detail: the heavy rhythm of footsteps coming up fast behind him, shouted commands, the scrape and impact of bodies moving in a tight space. What stayed with him most was not a clean sequence he could retell from beginning to end, but bursts of sensory experience that still arrive with unusual force. When he tries to explain exactly what happened, he starts, doubles back, loses the thread, and often stops in frustration, saying that the memory is vivid in his mind but impossible to lay out clearly in words.

In the weeks after, he found that reminders did not feel like reminders so much as a return. Footsteps behind him were especially potent. On the sidewalk, in a hallway, or while entering the newsroom, the sound of someone approaching from the rear could make the event feel as if it were happening again in the present. He would hear, in his head, sounds from that day layered over what was actually around him. Certain songs also began to unsettle him. If one came on in a store, in a rideshare, or from a coworker’s phone, his whole body tensed before he had fully registered why. He could not shake the sense that ordinary moments could suddenly become dangerous.

Because his work as a journalist requires attention, mobility, and comfort in unpredictable settings, these changes have been especially painful for him. He now has difficulty concentrating even on assignments he once would have handled easily. In editorial meetings he notices himself drifting, then scanning the room instead of listening. When he is sent somewhere unfamiliar, he feels immediate resistance. He has come to believe that if he cannot quickly assess a place, he is exposed in a way he cannot tolerate. He takes longer routes to avoid neighborhoods, buildings, or venues he does not know, and when he cannot avoid them he is on guard the entire time. He checks behind him frequently, on the street and even inside buildings, with the certainty that someone may be following him. At work this has made interviews more difficult and field reporting less reliable, and he is painfully aware of that change. He says he is no longer capable of doing the things that defined him.

Over time his efforts to get through the day have narrowed his life further. He wears concealing clothing so he will not be noticed, preferring loose layers and clothing that lets him blend in rather than stand out. He avoids anything that reminds him of someone he has lost, steering away from places, objects, and conversations that could bring grief into the room. More than that, he has started avoiding almost anything that might stir strong feeling at all, whether negative or positive. He skips music, pulls back from social outings, and keeps even good moments muted because emotional intensity itself feels risky. His girlfriend has noticed how shut down he has become. He is physically present but harder to reach, less spontaneous, less able to enjoy closeness or talk openly about what is happening.

What weighs on him now is not only fear but a bleak view of who he has become. He says he used to be a happy person and now feels miserable almost all the time. He speaks as though the event drew a line through his life, and that what came after has been wreckage. The conviction that his life has been destroyed by the trauma sits alongside the humiliating experience of no longer trusting his own mind to stay focused, no longer trusting himself in unfamiliar places, and no longer being able to tell the story of what happened in a way that feels coherent. He finally sought help after recognizing that these patterns were no longer easing with time and were beginning to threaten both his relationship and the career he most values. What frightens him most is that this diminished version of himself may be permanent. What he hopes for, even if he says it cautiously, is to feel like himself again in the world he once moved through with ease.
